title: The Warrior from Edom and a Prayer for Mercy
summary: A lone warrior strides in from Edom with garments stained red and explains that he has trodden the winepress of judgment by himself, because no one else would help. The chapter then turns to a long prayer that remembers God's kindness at the exodus, confesses Israel's rebellion, and pleads with God as Father to look down and act for his ruined sanctuary.
story: The last movement of Isaiah (chapters 56 to 66) speaks to a people waiting for the full restoration God promised in chapters 40 to 55. Chapters 60 to 62 have painted Zion's glory: nations streaming to her light, a herald anointed to proclaim good news, a city renamed as God's delight. Chapter 63 opens with the dark side of that same day. Before Zion can be vindicated, her enemies must be judged, and the warrior who does it acts alone. Then, from verse 7, the tone shifts completely. The people pray. The prayer that begins here runs through the end of chapter 64, and chapters 65 and 66 are God's answer. So this chapter stands at a turning point: after the vision of glory, the community admits how far it is from that vision and asks God to come.
historical:
Isaiah 56 to 66 addresses a community for whom Jerusalem's sanctuary has been trampled by enemies (63:18) and the temple burned (64:11). Many scholars date these chapters to the decades after the first exiles returned from Babylon in 538 BC, when the temple lay in ruins or was only slowly being rebuilt (it was completed about 515 BC), and they speak of this material as Third Isaiah. Those who hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book read these chapters as prophecy that looks ahead to the exile and beyond, voicing the prayer of a future generation. Either way, the chapter assumes the destruction Babylon brought in 587 or 586 BC.

Edom, the land southeast of the Dead Sea descended in Israel's memory from Esau, Jacob's brother, had a long and bitter history with Judah. Psalm 137:7 and the book of Obadiah remember Edom gloating and joining in when Jerusalem fell, and in the following centuries Edomites moved into southern Judah. Bozrah was one of Edom's chief cities. By the time of this oracle Edom had become a byword for the hostile nations as a whole, just as it is in Isaiah 34, where Bozrah is also named.
cultural:
Winemaking in ancient Israel happened in a winepress cut into rock or built of stone: grapes were heaped into an upper vat and trodden underfoot, and the juice ran through a channel into a lower vat. Treaders sang and shouted at harvest, and their legs and clothes were splashed red. Prophets used the image for judgment (Joel 3:13 and Lamentations 1:15 do the same), and the listener would picture the splatter immediately. There is also wordplay in the Hebrew: Edom sounds like adom, red, and Bozrah sounds like the word for a grape harvest, so the place names themselves anticipate the red garments and the vintage.

The prayer that follows draws on Israel's deepest memories. The shepherds of the flock are Moses and his fellow leaders; the Angel of His Presence recalls the angel who went before Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 23:20-23 and 33:14). Calling God Father was rare in Israel's prayers, and here it carries the sense of the one who made and redeemed a people and is responsible for them. Few ancient readers would miss the boldness of verse 17, which asks why God has let his people stray, as though only he could turn them back.
literary: The chapter has two unequal parts. Verses 1 to 6 are a dialogue in poetry, a question and answer like a watchman's challenge at a city gate: Who is this? Why are your clothes red? The answers come in the first person, and their key phrases (alone, no one to help, My arm brought Me salvation) repeat almost word for word Isaiah 59:16-17, which pictured God putting on righteousness as armor. Verses 7 to 19 begin a communal lament, a prayer form familiar from the Psalms (compare Psalms 44, 74, and 89), that moves from remembering God's past kindness, through confession, to the anguished question "Where is He" and a direct plea for help. The lament does not end at 63:19; it continues seamlessly into chapter 64.

outline.t: The lone warrior returns from Edom
Rebellion, and memory of the exodus
Plea to the Father to look down and return

doctrines.note: The warrior's red garments show God's judgment as real and terrible, carried out against those who oppose his purposes. It is paired with redemption in the same breath: the day of vengeance and the year of redemption arrive together, because rescuing the oppressed means defeating the oppressor.

This chapter and Psalm 51:11 are the only places in the Old Testament that speak of God's Holy Spirit in these words. The Spirit is grieved by rebellion, was set among the people at the exodus, and gave them rest, language that treats the Spirit as personally present rather than as an impersonal force.

The prayer models how God's people can speak to him after failure: recalling his character, confessing sin honestly, and then pressing their claim on him as Father and Redeemer, even to the point of asking why he has hidden himself.

words.note: Chesed, rendered here as loving devotion. It names loyal, covenant love, the steadfast kindness that keeps faith with a relationship even when the other party fails. The prayer opens with it (verse 7) because the whole plea rests on it: the people have no claim of their own, only the character of the God who bound himself to them.

Gaal, to redeem. The redeemer in Israel was the next of kin who bought back family land, freed a relative from slavery, or avenged a wrong. Isaiah uses the word often for God as Israel's kinsman. Verse 16 makes it a name, our Redeemer from Everlasting, and ties it to Father: God acts for this people because they belong to him.

Atsav, to hurt or grieve. The word is used for real emotional pain, including the grief God felt over human wickedness before the flood (Genesis 6:6). That the Holy Spirit can be grieved (verse 10) is striking; Paul echoes the phrase in Ephesians 4:30 when he tells believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God.

christ: Revelation 19:13-15 takes up this chapter's image when it describes the rider on the white horse, named the Word of God, dressed in a robe dipped in blood, who treads the winepress of the fury of God's wrath (see also Revelation 14:19-20). The New Testament thus presents the returning Christ as the warrior who acts alone to judge evil and rescue his people. Many readers have also connected the phrase I have trodden the winepress alone with the cross, where Jesus bore judgment with no one to help him, though Isaiah's warrior is stained with his enemies' blood, not his own, and that link is thematic rather than exegetical. In the prayer, the memory of God who shared his people's distress and carried them (verse 9) finds its fullest answer in the Son who took flesh and bore our griefs, and the plea to rend the heavens and come down, which follows directly in 64:1, is one Christians believe God answered in Jesus.

hard.q: How can the God of love be pictured spattered with blood, trampling nations in his anger?
hard.a:
The image is violent on purpose, and readers should not soften it. Three things help to read it well. First, it is poetry drawing on the harvest, a symbolic picture of decisive judgment rather than a battle report; Edom stands for every power that has crushed God's people. Second, the anger is not a mood but justice: the warrior acts because he looked and there was no one to help, so the judgment is the other side of rescue for the oppressed. A God who never opposed cruelty would not be good. Third, the Bible places such judgment in God's hands alone, not in human hands; it is a reason for the oppressed to hope, not a license for anyone to take vengeance.

Some readers still find the picture troubling, and Christians differ on how final and how literal such judgment is. The New Testament does not retreat from it, since Revelation reuses it for Christ, but it also shows the same Christ bearing judgment himself so that enemies can become friends. The chapter's own movement, from the warrior to a prayer for mercy, suggests that the right response to the vision of judgment is to ask God to save.

questions: The warrior says he looked and no one helped. Why does it matter that salvation and justice come from God acting alone rather than from human effort?
The prayer begins by remembering God's kindness before it confesses sin. How does remembering what God has done change the way you confess?
Verse 10 says the people grieved God's Holy Spirit. What do you make of the idea that God can be grieved, and how might it shape the way you live?
